title: Flawed Calculation in getNextAllowedVotingTimes
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/governance/contracts/VoteWeighting.sol#L779-L805
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/governance/contracts/VoteWeighting.sol#L804


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
[getNextAllowedVotingTimes](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/governance/contracts/VoteWeighting.sol#L779-L805) will return an incorrect next allowed voting time for voters who have never voted for a particular nominee. 

**This can lead to two potential problems:**

**`Allowing voters to vote too early`** If the `lastUserVote[voters[i]][nomineeHash]` is `0`, adding `WEIGHT_VOTE_DELAY` to it will result in a next allowed voting time that is equal to `WEIGHT_VOTE_DELAY`. This means that the voter will be allowed to vote immediately after the function call, even though they have never voted for that nominee before. This violates the intended behavior of enforcing a delay between votes for the same nominee.

**`Underflow issue`** If `WEIGHT_VOTE_DELAY` is a large value (e.g., a year or more), adding it to `0` can cause an underflow in the `uint256` data type, resulting in an extremely large value for the next allowed voting time. This can effectively lock the voter out from voting for that nominee for an extended period.

## Proof of Concept
Suppose we have the following setup:

`WEIGHT_VOTE_DELAY` is set to `365 days` (approximately one year)
Voter `0x1234...` has never voted for the nominee with the hash `0x5678...`
The current block timestamp is `1677628800` (March 1, 2023, 00:00:00 UTC)

When calling `getNextAllowedVotingTimes` with the nominee hash `0x5678...` and the voter `0x1234...`, the function will calculate the next allowed voting time as follows:
```solidity
nextAllowedVotingTimes[i] = lastUserVote[0x1234...][0x5678...] + WEIGHT_VOTE_DELAY;
                           = 0 + 365 days;
                           = 0;
```
Due to the underflow issue, the next allowed voting time is calculated as `0`, which means the voter `0x1234...` will be allowed to vote immediately, even though they have never voted for that nominee before.

Ref Code: [getNextAllowedVotingTimes#L804](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/governance/contracts/VoteWeighting.sol#L804)
```solidity
nextAllowedVotingTimes[i] = lastUserVote[voters[i]][nomineeHash] + WEIGHT_VOTE_DELAY;
```
This line assumes that `lastUserVote[voters[i]][nomineeHash]` is always initialized and has a valid value. However, if a voter has never voted for a particular nominee before, the `lastUserVote` mapping will not have an entry for that voter-nominee combination.

In such cases, the value of `lastUserVote[voters[i]][nomineeHash]` will be the default value of `uint256`, which is `0`. Adding `WEIGHT_VOTE_DELAY` to `0` will result in an incorrect next allowed voting time.

## Tools Used
Vs

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Check if `lastUserVote[voters[i]][nomineeHash]` is `0` and handle the case where the voter has never voted for the nominee before is using the current block timestamp as the starting point for the next allowed voting time if `lastUserVote[voters[i]][nomineeHash]` is `0`.
```solidity
nextAllowedVotingTimes[i] = lastUserVote[voters[i]][nomineeHash] > 0
    ? lastUserVote[voters[i]][nomineeHash] + WEIGHT_VOTE_DELAY
    : block.timestamp + WEIGHT_VOTE_DELAY;
```
This way, if `lastUserVote[voters[i]][nomineeHash]` is `0` (i.e., the voter has never voted for the nominee before), the next allowed voting time will be calculated based on the current block timestamp plus the `WEIGHT_VOTE_DELAY`.


## Assessed type

Math

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/registries/contracts/staking/StakingBase.sol#L464-L473


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In the second loop where the services are being evicted from the global set of staked services. The `serviceIndexes` array this occurs when the loop variable `i` becomes 0, and the code tries to access `serviceIndexes[i - 1]`, which is equivalent to `serviceIndexes[-1]`. Accessing an array with a negative index is an invalid operation and can cause unexpected behavior or even a runtime exception.

If this bug is triggered, it can lead to the following:

1. In the worst case, if the invalid memory access happens to modify critical data structures or contract state, it could compromise the integrity of the staking system.

Referenced Code: [_evict#L464-L472](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/registries/contracts/staking/StakingBase.sol#L464-L473)
```solidity
for (uint256 i = numEvictServices; i > 0; --i) {
    // ...
    uint256 idx = serviceIndexes[i - 1];
    // ...
}
```
In this loop, `i` starts from `numEvictServices` and decrements until it reaches `1`. However, when `i` becomes `0`, the expression `i - 1` evaluates to `-1`, leading to an out-of-bounds access attempt on the `serviceIndexe`s array.

## Proof of Concept
Let's consider a scenario where `numEvictServices` is 3, and the `serviceIndexes` array contains the following values: `[1, 2, 3]`.

When the loop starts, `i` is initially 3, and the code executes as expected:

  - `i = 3`: `serviceIndexes[i - 1]` evaluates to `serviceIndexes[2]`, which is valid and accesses the element at index 2.

As the loop continues, `i` decrements:

  - `i = 2`: `serviceIndexes[i - 1]` evaluates to `serviceIndexes[1]`, which is valid and accesses the element at index 1.
  - `i = 1`: `serviceIndexes[i - 1]` evaluates to `serviceIndexes[0]`, which is valid and accesses the element at index 0.

However, when `i` becomes 0, the problematic behavior occurs:

  - `i = 0`: `serviceIndexes[i - 1]` evaluates to `serviceIndexes[-1]`, which is an invalid index and triggers an out-of-bounds access attempt.

At this point, the code may throw a runtime exception or exhibit undefined behavior.

## Tools Used
Vs

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Modify the loop condition to iterate until `i` is greater than or equal to 1, like this:
```solidity
for (uint256 i = numEvictServices; i >= 1; --i) {
    // ...
    uint256 idx = serviceIndexes[i - 1];
    // ...
}
```



## Assessed type

Other

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/registries/contracts/staking/StakingBase.sol#L507-L511


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In the `_claim` function, the code does not update the `sInfo.nonces` value after claiming the reward. The `nonces` field is likely used to track the number of times rewards have been claimed for a service. By not incrementing it after a successful claim, it may lead to inconsistencies or incorrect tracking of the claiming process.

Referenced Code: [#StakingBase.sol:507-511](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/registries/contracts/staking/StakingBase.sol#L507-L511)
```solidity
// Transfer accumulated rewards to the service multisig
// Note that the reentrancy is not possible since the reward is set to zero
address multisig = sInfo.multisig;
_withdraw(multisig, reward);

emit RewardClaimed(epochCounter, serviceId, msg.sender, multisig, sInfo.nonces, reward);
```
We can see, the `sInfo.nonces` value is not incremented after the `_withdraw` function call, which transfers the rewards to the service's multisig address. This missing increment is the root cause of the inconsistencies and potential issues described above.

The `RewardClaimed` event emitted at the end of the `_claim` function includes the `sInfo.nonces` value. Suppose this value is not incremented after a successful claim. In that case, the emitted event will contain an incorrect nonces value, providing misleading information to event listeners or off-chain systems that rely on these events for tracking and monitoring purposes.

## Proof of Concept
Imagine a scenario where a service owner claims rewards multiple times without the `nonces` value being incremented.

1. Initial state:

  - Service ID: 1
  - Service owner: 0xABC...
  - Rewards: 100 tokens
  - Nonces: 0

2. First reward claim:

  - Service owner calls `_claim(1, true)`
  - Rewards (100 tokens) are transferred to the service's multisig address
  - Nonces remains at 0
  - Event emitted: `RewardClaimed(epochCounter, 1, 0xABC..., multisig, 0, 100)`

3. Second reward claim:

  - Service owner calls `_claim(1, true)` again
  - Rewards (0 tokens) are transferred to the service's multisig address (assuming no new rewards have been added)
  - Nonces still remains at 0
  - Event emitted: `RewardClaimed(epochCounter, 1, 0xABC..., multisig, 0, 0)`

In this scenario, the service owner was able to claim rewards multiple times without the value of the `nonce` being incremented, leading to inconsistent tracking and incorrect emission of events.

## Tools Used
Vs
StakingBase.sol:478-511
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
We should increment the `sInfo.nonces` value after the reward has been successfully transferred.
```solidity
// Transfer accumulated rewards to the service multisig
// Note that the reentrancy is not possible since the reward is set to zero
address multisig = sInfo.multisig;
_withdraw(multisig, reward);

// Increment the nonces value
sInfo.nonces++;

emit RewardClaimed(epochCounter, serviceId, msg.sender, multisig, sInfo.nonces, reward);
```
By incrementing `sInfo.nonces` after the `_withdraw function` call, we ensure that the nonces value is properly updated to reflect the successful reward claim.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/tokenomics/contracts/staking/ArbitrumDepositProcessorL1.sol#L174


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Failure to bridge tokens to other contract of L2 from L1

## Proof of Concept
Olas uses `approve` that do not handle non-standard erc20 behavior. Acc: to weird ERC20 repo

> Some token contracts do not return any value.
> Some token contracts revert the transaction when the allowance is not zero.

One such instance from [ArbitrumDepositProcessorL1](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/tokenomics/contracts/staking/ArbitrumDepositProcessorL1.sol#L174)
```
        if (transferAmount > 0) {
            // Approve tokens for the bridge contract
            IToken(olas).approve(l1ERC20Gateway, transferAmount);

```
If one such token is USDT[which doesn't return any value and has a approval race condition of not approving amt1 >0 when amt0>0 is already approved] / Tether Gold[returns false even if transfers are succesfull], so it may lead the user to believe that the tokens has not been approved and they may approve it again , sending double amount or end up reverting


## Tools Used
None

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use solmate `safeApprove` instead and set the allowance to 0 before calling it. 

> *Note:* The recommendation should be applied to all such instances{ [1](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/tokenomics/contracts/staking/GnosisDepositProcessorL1.sol#L65), [2](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/tokenomics/contracts/staking/OptimismDepositProcessorL1.sol#L111), [3](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/tokenomics/contracts/staking/PolygonDepositProcessorL1.sol#L68)}

title: Incorrect inflation amounts and rates calculation for OLAS token for initial 9 years
warden_comment: # Lines of code https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/main/tokenomics/contracts/TokenomicsConstants.sol#L33-L102 # Vulnerability details ## Impact Incorrect inflation rate computation for OLAS token leads to minting imprecise amount of OLAS tokens each year. As stated in the whitepaper, OLAS is an [inflationary token](https://olas.network/documents/whitepaper/Autonolas_Tokenomics_Core_Technical_Document.pdf), meaning its minting process is gradual rather than instantaneous (such as through token initialization) and the inflation is meant to be controlled. > OLAS follows an inflationary model that accounts for the economic primitives enabled by this tokenomics, such as the bonding mechanism and specific OLAS top-ups, e.g. extra incentives that developers can eventually receive. During the first 10 years, 47.35% of the total token supply (1 billion) is projected to be issued via bonding and component/agent top-ups. The technical aspects of the inflation rate calculations are described using the following parameters: | |Parameter Name|Parameter Definition|Value in Whitepaper| |-|:-|:-:|:-:| | [P‑01] | First year inflation rate | The percentage of the initial token supply that is minted during the year of the OLAS token launch | 0.6% | | [P‑02] | Second year inflation rate | The percentage of the token supply that is minted during the second year | 7.2% | | [P‑03] | Initial inflation rate | The percentage of the token supply that is minted for the third year | 12.5% | | [P‑04] | Dis-inflation rate | The rate with which inflation is decreased every year in the range comprising year 3 to year 9 | 16% | | [P‑05] | Long-term inflation rate | Tokens minted in the long run | 2% | Thus, we can infer that the inflation rates are variable and indeed obey this behavior: The inflation rate for the OLAS token drastically increases during the initial three years, then stabilizes to a moderate pace for the subsequent six years. This pattern underscores the critical need for precise annual token minting. Any imprecision could break the invariant, leading to an uncontrollable inflation process. Therefore, maintaining accuracy in the token minting process each year is essential to ensure the system's stability. The inflation rate calculations are implemented inside the `TokenomicsConstants` contract which is used in the `Tokenomics` contract: ```Solidity function getInflationForYear(uint256 numYears) public pure returns (uint256 inflationAmount) { // For the first 10 years the inflation caps are pre-defined as differences between next year cap and current year one if (numYears < 10) { // Initial OLAS allocation is 526_500_000_0e17 uint88[10] memory inflationAmounts = [ 3_159_000e18, 40_254_084e18, 40_400_000e18, 56_000_000e18, 80_000_000e18, 72_000_000e18, 64_000_000e18, 48_000_000e18, 40_000_000e18, 29_686_916e18 ]; ... } ``` Also, the inflation cap for a specific year is calculated via `getSupplyCapForYear()` which are derived from the inflation rate amounts. To calculate the inflation amounts, supply caps, and inflation rates, the following relationships are used (with inflation rates presented in percentages): $$ inflation \ rate = \frac{next \ year \ cap - current \ year \ cap}{current \ year \ cap} $$ $$ supply \ cap = (current \ year \ cap * (1 + \frac{inflation \ rate}{100})) $$ and: $$ inflation \ Amount = next \ year \ cap - current \ year \ cap $$ Considering the inflation parameters presented in the table above, we calculate the mentioned parameters using the data provided in the smart contracts: (Initial OLAS allocation is `526_500_000e18`) $$ First \ year \ inflation \ rate = \frac{3159000 \times 10^{18}}{526500000 \times 10^{18}} = 0.6 \\% $$ $$ First \ year \ supply \ cap = 3159000 \times 10^{18} + 526500000 \times 10^{18} = 529659000 \times 10^{18} $$ $$ Second \ year \ inflation \ rate = \frac{40254084 \times 10^{18}}{529659000 \times 10^{18}} = 7.6 \\% $$ $$ Second \ year \ supply \ cap = 40254084 \times 10^{18} + 529659000 \times 10^{18} = 569913084 \times 10^{18} $$ Here, the Initial inflation rate is calculated according to this definition: > [The percentage of the token supply that is minted for the third year](https://olas.network/documents/whitepaper/Autonolas_Tokenomics_Core_Technical_Document.pdf) $$ Initial \ inflation \ rate = \frac{40400000 \times 10^{18}}{569913084 \times 10^{18}} = 7 \\% $$ $$ Third \ year \ supply \ cap = 40400000 \times 10^{18} + 569913084 \times 10^{18} = 610313084 \times 10^{18} $$ Even if we calculate the Initial inflation rate based on the total tokens minted till the end of the third year, we will get: $$ Initial \ inflation \ rate = \frac{(3159000 + 40254084 + 40400000) \times 10^{18}}{526500000 \times 10^{18}} = 15.9 \\% $$ I keep this one as the initial inflation rate here. Also for the fourth year, the inflation rate is calculated as 9.17%, which is equal to a 42% reduction compared to 15.9%. | |Parameter Name|Value in Smart Contract|Value in Whitepaper| |-|:-|:-:|:-:| | [P‑01] | First year inflation rate | 0.6% | 0.6% | | [P‑02] | Second year inflation rate | 7.6% | 7.2% | | [P‑03] | Third year inflation rate | 7% | 12.5% | | [P‑04] | Fourth year inflation rate | 9.17% | 10.5% | | [P‑05] | Fifth year inflation rate | 12% | 8.5% | | [P‑06] | Sixth year inflation rate | 9.6% | 7.6% | | [P‑07] | Seventh year inflation rate | 7.8% | 6.8% | | [P‑08] | Eight year inflation rate | 5.4% | 5.4% | | [P‑08] | Ninth year inflation rate | 4.3% | 4.3% | The current inflation rates and amounts defined in `TokenomicsConstants` are inaccurate. The values provided in the table allow us to make a clear comparison, highlighting the discrepancies: If the image above is not displayed, you can manually check it in [this address](https://github.com/MatinR1/MatinR1/blob/main/InflationRates.png) The red line shows the whitepaper-based inflation rates, while the blue line shows the current behavior which is implemented in the smart contracts. This figure shows the large discrepancy between the implemented values inside the contracts and the whitepaper. This will result in the minting of inaccurate token amounts, disrupting the protocol's invariant and leading to uncontrollable inflation. ## Tools Used Manual Review ## Recommended Mitigation Steps Consider modifying the inflation amounts and supply caps for the initial nine years inside the `TokenomicsConstants` contract. ## Assessed type Other

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/registries/contracts/staking/StakingFactory.sol#L168


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
There is a vulnerability in the createStakingInstance function, which uses the create2 method for creating staking contract instances. The vulnerability arises from the use of a salt based on the blockchain ID and an incrementing nonce, making the code susceptible to block reorganization (reorg) attacks.

Vulnerability Description
The createStakingInstance function generates a new staking contract instance using the create2 method. The salt for this operation is derived from the blockchain ID and an incrementing nonce. Since the blockchain ID remains constant within a single blockchain, the salt's uniqueness relies solely on the nonce, which increments with each new contract creation. This dependency on the incrementing nonce makes the function vulnerable to block reorg attacks.

Code Snippet
The relevant code section is shown below:

```
uint256 localNonce = nonce;
// Get salt based on chain Id and nonce values
bytes32 salt = keccak256(abi.encodePacked(block.chainid, localNonce));
// Get the deployment data based on the proxy bytecode and the implementation address
bytes memory deploymentData = abi.encodePacked(type(StakingProxy).creationCode,
    uint256(uint160(implementation)));

// solhint-disable-next-line no-inline-assembly
assembly {
    instance := create2(0x0, add(0x20, deploymentData), mload(deploymentData), salt)
}
// Check that the proxy creation was successful
if (instance == address(0)) {
    revert ProxyCreationFailed(implementation);
}

```


A blockchain reorganization (reorg) occurs when a longer or more valid chain of blocks replaces the current chain, causing some blocks to be discarded and transactions to be reordered. Reorgs can lead to inconsistencies in transaction processing and are more common in proof-of-stake (PoS) blockchains, where reorgs can reach significant depths.

Attack Scenario
An attacker can exploit this vulnerability by performing the following steps:

Initial Contract Creation: The attacker observes the nonce value used for the latest contract creation and waits for a transaction that creates a new staking instance.

Blockchain Reorganization: During a block reorg, the attacker's malicious transactions are included in a longer chain, invalidating the original chain where the legitimate contract creation was intended.

Front-Running the Nonce: The attacker quickly submits a transaction using the same nonce value as the original transaction. Since the nonce has been incremented, the attacker's transaction gets the intended salt.

Deployment of Malicious Contract: The attacker successfully deploys their malicious staking contract instance with the same salt, resulting in the overwriting or duplication of contract addresses.

Exploitation: Users that has interacted with the first legitimate instance, unknowingly have now sent funds or staked in the malicious contract. This allows the attacker to siphon funds or perform other malicious actions.

## Proof of Concept
Examples of other findings of this issue or similar:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-abracadabra-money-findings/issues/211


https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-amphora-findings/issues/233


https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-01-rabbithole-findings/issues/661


## Tools Used

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Make salt more unique by including msg.sender for example 


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/main/tokenomics/contracts/staking/WormholeDepositProcessorL1.sol#L85


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Wormhole has a refund mechanism that refunds on the destination chain instead of the source as the `refundChain` passed by default is L2, but `WormholeDepositProcessorL1::_sendMessage` passes `msg.sender` as a refunder, resulting in all the refunds being sent to the wrong recipient.

## Proof of Concept

In case no explicit `refundAccount` has been provided to the `bridgePayload` `msg.sender` , which is the `Dispenser` contract, will be used by default. The problem is that since `Dispenser` is a smart contract, it won’t have the same address on the L2 chains where the refund will happen. This will result in all the ever-refunded tokens being sent to a random recipient on the L2 chain when the refund happens.

```solidity
/// @inheritdoc DefaultDepositProcessorL1
  function _sendMessage(
      address[] memory targets,
      uint256[] memory stakingIncentives,
      bytes memory bridgePayload,
      uint256 transferAmount
  ) internal override returns (uint256 sequence) {
...MORE CODE
      // If refundAccount is zero, default to msg.sender
      if (refundAccount == address(0)) {
          refundAccount = msg.sender;
      }

      sequence = sendTokenWithPayloadToEvm(
          uint16(wormholeTargetChainId), 
          l2TargetDispenser, 
          data, 
          0,
          gasLimitMessage, 
          olas,//REVIEW this should be set to the address of Olas on the destination chain
          transferAmount, 
          uint16(l2TargetChainId), 
          refundAccount);//@audit wrong address
  }
```

Refunds in Wormhole are for the unused gas on the destination chain execution. We say that refunds will be happening often as the  `gasLimitMessage` is an arbitrary parameter provided from the caller as well, although having better validation.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Revert the transaction in case `address(0)` is passed as `refundAddress` to the `bridgePayload`.


## Assessed type

Token-Transfer

# Vulnerability details

## details of the bug 
The  flaw in its receive function, is where any funds sent to the contract are directly added to the availableRewards balance. and This can lead to an overestimation of available rewards, and  causing the contract to distribute more rewards than intended. this is a bug  that is arises from the incorrect assumption that all incoming funds are meant to be rewards, which might not always be the case. This flaw can affect the contract's financial stability and reward distribution logic.
```solidity
   receive() external payable {
        // Add to the contract and available rewards balances
        uint256 newBalance = balance + msg.value;
        uint256 newAvailableRewards = availableRewards + msg.value;

        // Record the new actual balance and available rewards
        balance = newBalance;
        availableRewards = newAvailableRewards;
```
## Impact
This can lead to an overestimation of available rewards, which can cause the contract to distribute more rewards than intend
## root of the bug : 
The receive function updates both the balance and availableRewards with any funds received. This behavior assumes all incoming funds are for rewards distribution, without verifying the purpose of the transaction. As a result, any funds sent to the contract, regardless of intent, will be treated as rewards, leading to potential overestimation of available rewards.

- an Example show the Bug:
- let's say we have this :
- Initial availableRewards is 2 ETH.
- A user or external entity sends 1 ETH to the contract for purposes other than rewards a deposit or accidental transfer .
- The receive function is triggered, which updates availableRewards to 3 ETH.
- The contract now incorrectly assumes there are 3 ETH available for rewards, leading to an overestimation.
- During reward distribution, the contract may allocate 3 ETH instead of the correct 2 ETH, over-distributing by 1 ETH.

need to ensuring that only intended funds are added to availableRewards

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/tokenomics/contracts/staking/WormholeDepositProcessorL1.sol#L96
https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/wormhole-solidity-sdk/blob/b9e129e65d34827d92fceeed8c87d3ecdfc801d0/src/TokenBase.sol#L145
https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/wormhole-solidity-sdk/blob/b9e129e65d34827d92fceeed8c87d3ecdfc801d0/src/interfaces/IWormholeRelayer.sol#L159


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Messages cannot be send on WormholeDepositProcessorL1.sol as it doesn't forward the needed native token to cover the cost of the `quoteEVMDeliveryPrice` when sending token with payload. This will cause the function to alsways fail.

## Proof of Concept

The `_sendMessage` function allows for sending token and or messages to L2. In WormholeDepositProcessorL1.sol, this is done by querying the `sendTokenWithPayloadToEvm` function in wormhole's TokenBase.sol. `_sendMessage` however doesn't however forward any native token to wormhole, hence there are no tokens available to cover the cost of sending.

```solidity
    function _sendMessage(
        address[] memory targets,
        uint256[] memory stakingIncentives,
        bytes memory bridgePayload,
        uint256 transferAmount
    ) internal override returns (uint256 sequence) {
        .....
        sequence = sendTokenWithPayloadToEvm(uint16(wormholeTargetChainId), l2TargetDispenser, data, 0,
            gasLimitMessage, olas, transferAmount, uint16(l2TargetChainId), refundAccount);
    }
```

When we look at `sendTokenWithPayloadToEvm` in wormhole, we find that the cost of sending is queried with `quoteEVMDeliveryPrice` function and is then expected to be forwarded to the relayer through the `sendVaasToEvm` function.

```solidity
    function sendTokenWithPayloadToEvm(
        uint16 targetChain,
        address targetAddress,
        bytes memory payload,
        uint256 receiverValue,
        uint256 gasLimit,
        address token,
        uint256 amount,
        uint16 refundChain,
        address refundAddress
    ) internal returns (uint64) {
        VaaKey[] memory vaaKeys = new VaaKey[](1);
        vaaKeys[0] = transferTokens(token, amount, targetChain, targetAddress);

        (uint256 cost, ) = wormholeRelayer.quoteEVMDeliveryPrice(
            targetChain,
            receiverValue,
            gasLimit
        );
        return
            wormholeRelayer.sendVaasToEvm{value: cost}(
                targetChain,
                targetAddress,
                payload,
                receiverValue,
                gasLimit,
                vaaKeys,
                refundChain,
                refundAddress
            );
    }
}
```

Due to native token not being sent when sending message, the `sendTokenWithPayloadToEvm` call will fail causing the `sendVaasToEvm` to fail an causing the entire function to revert as there's not enough tokens to cover the delivery cost.

## Tools Used
Manual code review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider calculating the needed cost and forwarding the sent ETH to wormhole too.
```solidity
        sequence = sendTokenWithPayloadToEvm{value: cost}(uint16(wormholeTargetChainId), l2TargetDispenser, data, 0,
            gasLimitMessage, olas, transferAmount, uint16(l2TargetChainId), refundAccount);
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/tokenomics/contracts/Dispenser.sol#L756-L759


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
```solidity
// Check for the retainer hash
if (retainerHash == nomineeHash) {
    revert WrongAccount(retainer);
}
```
The purpose of this check seems to be preventing the removal of the retainer account. However, the check is comparing the `retainerHash` with the `nomineeHash`. If the `nomineeHash` happens to match the `retainerHash`, the function will revert with the `WrongAccount` error, even if the `nomineeHash` does not correspond to the actual retainer address.

## Proof of Concept
The bug in the `removeNominee` function allows for the unintended removal of the retainer account. If an attacker manages to find a `nomineeHash` that matches the `retainerHash`, they can exploit this vulnerability to remove the retainer account from the system, even though the `nomineeHash` does not correspond to the actual retainer address.

[tokenomics/contracts/Dispenser.sol#L756-L758](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/tokenomics/contracts/Dispenser.sol#L756-L759)
```solidity
// Check for the retainer hash
if (retainerHash == nomineeHash) {
    revert WrongAccount(retainer);
}
```
**Explanation:** The purpose of this code snippet is to prevent the removal of the retainer account. The `retainerHash` is likely a stored hash value representing the retainer account, while the `nomineeHash` is the hash of the account that is being removed.

However, the issue lies in the comparison between `retainerHash` and `nomineeHash`. The code is directly comparing these two hash values, assuming that if they match, the `nomineeHash` corresponds to the retainer account. But this assumption is flawed because hash collisions can occur.

In Solidity, the `==` operator compares the binary representation of the values. If two different inputs happen to have the same hash value (i.e., a hash collision), the condition `retainerHash == nomineeHash` will evaluate to `true`, even though the `nomineeHash` does not correspond to the retainer address.

An example:

  1. Suppose the `retainerHash` is set to a specific value, let's say 0x1234567890abcdef.
  2. An attacker finds an account with a different address, let's say `0xattackeraddress`, that happens to have the same hash value as `retainerHash` when hashed using the same hashing algorithm.
  3. The attacker calls the `removeNominee` function with the `nomineeHash` set to `0x1234567890abcdef`.
  4. The condition `retainerHash == nomineeHash` evaluates to true since both values are the same.
  5. The function reverts with the `WrongAccount` error, effectively removing the account associated with `0xattackeraddress`, even though it is not the actual retainer account.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The comparison should be made between the `nomineeHash` and the hash of the retainer address, rather than the `retainerHash`. 
```solidity
// Check for the retainer address
if (keccak256(abi.encodePacked(retainer)) == nomineeHash) {
    revert WrongAccount(retainer);
}
```
By hashing the `retainer` address using `keccak256` and comparing it with the `nomineeHash`, the function will correctly identify if the provided `nomineeHash` corresponds to the `retainer` address and revert accordingly.


## Assessed type

Access Control

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/tokenomics/contracts/Dispenser.sol#L1146-L1159


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In the loop that iterates over the epochs from `firstClaimedEpoch` to `lastClaimedEpoch`, the `totalReturnAmount` is calculated by multiplying `stakingPoint.stakingIncentive` with `stakingWeight`. However, `stakingWeight` is obtained from the `nomineeRelativeWeight` function of the `IVoteWeighting` contract, which likely returns a value with 18 decimal places (assuming it follows the common convention in Ethereum).

When `totalReturnAmount` is divided by `1e18` after the loop. This division is intended to remove the extra 18 decimal places, but it is done only once at the end of the loop. As a result, if there are multiple iterations in the loop, the `totalReturnAmount` will accumulate values with 18 decimal places in each iteration, leading to an incorrect final value.

## Proof of Concept
- Let's assume there are 3 epochs to iterate over, with the following values.
   - Epoch 1: `stakingPoint.stakingIncentive = 100`, `stakingWeight = 1e18`
   - Epoch 2: `stakingPoint.stakingIncentive = 200`, `stakingWeight = 1.5e18`
   - Epoch 3: `stakingPoint.stakingIncentive = 300`, `stakingWeight = 2e18`

- With the current implementation, the `totalReturnAmount` calculation would be.
   - Epoch 1: `totalReturnAmount = 100 * 1e18 = 100e18`
   - Epoch 2: `totalReturnAmount = 100e18 + 200 * 1.5e18 = 400e18`
   - Epoch 3: `totalReturnAmount = 400e18 + 300 * 2e18 = 1000e18`

- After the loop, `totalReturnAmount` is divided by `1e18`, resulting in `1000`.
-  However, the correct calculation should be:
   - Epoch 1: `totalReturnAmount = (100 * 1e18) / 1e18 = 100`
   - Epoch 2: `totalReturnAmount = 100 + (200 * 1.5e18) / 1e18 = 400`
   - Epoch 3: `totalReturnAmount = 400 + (300 * 2e18) / 1e18 = 1000`

The correct `totalReturnAmount` should be `1000`, but the current implementation yields `1000e18`, which is a significantly inflated value.

The affected code snippet: [tokenomics/contracts/Dispenser.sol#L1146-1159](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/tokenomics/contracts/Dispenser.sol#L1146-L1159)
```solidity
for (uint256 j = firstClaimedEpoch; j < lastClaimedEpoch; ++j) {
    // ...

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In this line of the syncWithheldAmount function: 
```solidity
uint256 withheldAmount = mapChainIdWithheldAmounts[chainId] + amount;
```
The problem is that the addition operation `mapChainIdWithheldAmounts[chainId] + amount` can overflow if the sum exceeds the maximum value that can be stored in a `uint256`. If an overflow occurs, the resulting `withheldAmount` will wrap around and have an incorrect value.

## Proof of Concept
[tokenomics/contracts/Dispenser.sol#L1183](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/tokenomics/contracts/Dispenser.sol#L1183)
```solidity
uint256 withheldAmount = mapChainIdWithheldAmounts[chainId] + amount;
```
This line performs an addition operation between the existing withheld amount stored in mapChainIdWithheldAmounts[chainId] and the new amount provided as a parameter. If the sum exceeds the maximum value that can be stored in a uint256, an overflow will occur.
1. Suppose the current value of mapChainIdWithheldAmounts[chainId] is 2^256 - 1 (the maximum value for uint256).
2. Now, if the syncWithheldAmount function is called with an amount greater than 0, the addition operation will overflow.
3. The resulting withheldAmount will wrap around and have a value that is significantly smaller than expected.

Here's code snippet that demonstrates the overflow:
```solidity
uint256 maxUint256 = type(uint256).max;
uint256 currentWithheldAmount = maxUint256;
uint256 newAmount = 1;

uint256 withheldAmount = currentWithheldAmount + newAmount;

// Expected: withheldAmount should be 0 (overflow)
// Actual: withheldAmount will be 0
```
In this example, currentWithheldAmount is set to the maximum value of uint256, and newAmount is set to 1. When the addition operation is performed, an overflow occurs, and the resulting withheldAmount wraps around to 0.

## Tools Used
Manual Review
tokenomics/contracts/Dispenser.sol#L1009
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
We can use the `SafeMath` library or the built-in Solidity overflow checks (if using Solidity version 0.8.0 or higher) to perform the addition safely.
```solidity
uint256 withheldAmount = mapChainIdWithheldAmounts[chainId].add(amount);
```
Using `SafeMath.add()`, the addition operation will revert if an overflow occurs, preventing the incorrect updating of the `withheldAmount`.

Alternatively, since we are using Solidity version 0.8.0 higher, we can rely on the built-in overflow checks by simply adding the unchecked keyword before the addition operation:
```solidity
unchecked {
    uint256 withheldAmount = mapChainIdWithheldAmounts[chainId] + amount;
}
```
This will disable the overflow check for that specific operation, allowing the code to handle the overflow manually if needed.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/tokenomics/contracts/Dispenser.sol#L1220-L1225


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The normalization of the `amount` when the `bridgingDecimals` is less than 18 in `syncWithheldAmountMaintenance` function: [tokenomics/contracts/Dispenser.sol#L1220-L1225](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/tokenomics/contracts/Dispenser.sol#L1220-L1225)
```solidity
if (bridgingDecimals < 18) {
    uint256 normalizedAmount = amount / (10 ** (18 - bridgingDecimals));
    normalizedAmount *= 10 ** (18 - bridgingDecimals);
    // Downsize staking incentive to a specified number of bridging decimals
    amount = normalizedAmount;
}
```
The issue is that the normalization process is incorrect. The current code divides `amount` by `10 ** (18 - bridgingDecimals)` and then multiplies the result by the same factor. This effectively cancels out the division and leaves `amount` unchanged.

1. Impact on Withheld Amounts:
   - The purpose of the `syncWithheldAmountMaintenance` function is to manually sync the withheld amount from L2 to L1 in case of a bridge failure scenario.
   - The bug in the normalization process fails to correctly adjust the amount when the `bridgingDecimals` is less than 18.
   - As a result, the withheld amount being synced will not be accurately represented in the L1 contract.
   - This can lead to discrepancies between the actual withheld amount on L2 and the recorded withheld amount on L1.

2. Incorrect Normalization:
   - The problem code attempts to normalize the `amount` based on the `bridgingDecimals`.
   - However, the normalization process is flawed because it divides `amount` by `10 ** (18 - bridgingDecimals)` and then multiplies the result by the same factor.
   - This effectively cancels out the division and leaves `amount` unchanged, defeating the purpose of normalization.
   - As a consequence, the `amount` is not correctly adjusted to the specified number of bridging decimals.

## Proof of Concept
* Let's consider an example:
  - Suppose `amount` is 1000 and `bridgingDecimals` is 6.
  - The expected normalized amount should be 1000 / (10 ** (18 - 6)) = 1000 / (10 ** 12) = 0.000001.
  - However, with the current bug, the normalization process will be:
   - `normalizedAmount` = 1000 / (10 ** (18 - 6)) = 0.000001
   - `normalizedAmount` *= 10 ** (18 - 6) = 0.000001 * (10 ** 12) = 1000

* The resulting `amount` remains unchanged at 1000, which is incorrect.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
We should remove the multiplication step.
```solidity
if (bridgingDecimals < 18) {
    uint256 normalizedAmount = amount / (10 ** (18 - bridgingDecimals));
    // Downsize staking incentive to a specified number of bridging decimals
    amount = normalizedAmount;
}
```
With this fix, the `amount` will be correctly normalized to the specified number of bridging decimals when `bridgingDecimals` is less than 18.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
tokenomics/contracts/Dispenser.sol#changeIncentiveFractions function assumes that the sum of `_rewardComponentFraction` and `_rewardAgentFraction` is always less than or equal to 100. Yet it doesn't enforce this condition properly. If the sum of these fractions is less than 100, the `rewardTreasuryFraction` will be calculated incorrectly.

Here's the line: [tokenomics/contracts/Dispenser.sol#L735](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/tokenomics/contracts/Tokenomics.sol#L735)
```solidity
tp.epochPoint.rewardTreasuryFraction = uint8(100 - _rewardComponentFraction - _rewardAgentFraction);
```
If `_rewardComponentFraction + _rewardAgentFraction` is less than 100, the `rewardTreasuryFraction` will be set to a value greater than the actual leftover fraction.

## Proof of Concept
[tokenomics/contracts/Dispenser.sol#changeIncentiveFractions](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/tokenomics/contracts/Tokenomics.sol#L703-L746)
If the sum of `_rewardComponentFraction` and `_rewardAgentFraction` is less than 100, the `rewardTreasuryFraction` will be set to a value greater than the actual leftover fraction. This means that the treasury will receive more rewards than intended, while the components and agents will receive less.

For example, let's say `_rewardComponentFraction` is 30 and `_rewardAgentFraction` is 50. The sum of these fractions is 80, which is less than 100. According to the current implementation, the `rewardTreasuryFraction` will be calculated as:
```solidity
tp.epochPoint.rewardTreasuryFraction = uint8(100 - _rewardComponentFraction - _rewardAgentFraction);
```
In this case, `rewardTreasuryFraction` will be set to 100 - 30 - 50 = 20. However, the actual leftover fraction should be 100 - 80 = 20, not 20.

This issue can lead to an incorrect distribution of rewards, favoring the treasury over the components and agents.

Referenced Code: tokenomics/contracts/Tokenomics.sol, lines 735-736
```solidity
// Rewards are always distributed in full: the leftovers will be allocated to treasury
tp.epochPoint.rewardTreasuryFraction = uint8(100 - _rewardComponentFraction - _rewardAgentFraction);
```

Consider the following scenario:

  1. The `changeIncentiveFractions` function is called with `_rewardComponentFraction = 30` and `_rewardAgentFraction = 50`.
  2. The function checks that the sum of these fractions is not greater than 100, which passes.
  3. The `rewardTreasuryFraction` is calculated as `100 - 30 - 50 = 20`.
  4. The `rewardTreasuryFraction` is set to 20, even though the actual leftover fraction should be `100 - (30 + 50) = 20`.

As a result, the treasury will receive 20% of the rewards, while it should only receive 20% based on the provided fractions.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Modify the check for the sum of fractions to ensure that it equals 100 exactly.
```solidity
if (_rewardComponentFraction + _rewardAgentFraction != 100) {
    revert WrongAmount(_rewardComponentFraction + _rewardAgentFraction, 100);
}
```
By changing the condition from `>` to `!=`, you ensure that the sum of `_rewardComponentFraction` and `_rewardAgentFraction` must be exactly 100. This way, there won't be any discrepancy in the calculation of `rewardTreasuryFraction`.

Additionally, you can remove the line that calculates `rewardTreasuryFraction` since it will always be zero if the fractions add up to 100:
```solidity
// Remove this line
// tp.epochPoint.rewardTreasuryFraction = uint8(100 - _rewardComponentFraction - _rewardAgentFraction);
```
By making these changes, I think we can ensure that the `changeIncentiveFractions` function works as intended and avoids any potential bugs related to the calculation of the treasury fraction.

# Vulnerability details

### Vulnerability Details: Dangerous Race Condition and Bad Practice in Array Handling

**Vulnerability Type:**
- Dangerous Race Condition
- Bad Practice in Array Handling

**Location in Code:**
- [VoteWeighting.sol#L621-L627](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/governance/contracts/VoteWeighting.sol#L621-L627)

**Description:**
The current implementation of removing the last element from the `setNominees` array and shuffling the elements can lead to dangerous race conditions and is considered a bad practice. This is because arrays are class properties and can be accessed and modified concurrently, leading to potential inconsistencies and unexpected behavior.

Here's the problematic section of the code:

```solidity
// Shuffle the current last nominee id in the set to be placed to the removed one
nominee = setNominees[setNominees.length - 1];
bytes32 replacedNomineeHash = keccak256(abi.encode(nominee));
mapNomineeIds[replacedNomineeHash] = id;
setNominees[id] = nominee;
// Pop the last element from the set
setNominees.pop();
```

### Issues Identified:

1. **Race Condition:**
   The access and modification of `setNominees` and `mapNomineeIds` without proper synchronization can lead to race conditions. Multiple concurrent calls to this code segment can result in corrupted state or unexpected behavior due to simultaneous reads and writes.

2. **Accessing and Popping from the Array:**
   The code assumes that `setNominees` is not empty without explicit checks, which can lead to runtime errors if `setNominees` is empty. This can disrupt the flow of the contract and result in failed transactions.

3. **Bad Practice in Array Handling:**
   Directly manipulating class properties without encapsulation or checks is a bad practice. It makes the code harder to maintain and reason about, especially in a concurrent execution environment like blockchain.

### Recommended Fix:

Implement a function to safely remove and return an element from the array while ensuring atomicity of operations. Here’s an improved version of the code:

for example usage of pop without specification of the desired element is not entirely safe. 

for example usage of setNominees.length - 1 at two individuals lines or essentially setNominees.length - 1 initially then finally pop() will not be entirely safe.

if this was a possibility for example where nominee = setNominees.pop(); will be preferred
if this was a possibility for example where nominee = setNominees.remove(index); will be preferred

```

### References:
- [VoteWeighting.sol#L621-L627](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/governance/contracts/VoteWeighting.sol#L621-L627)

### Potential Impact:
If not addressed, this vulnerability can lead to inconsistent state in the contract, unexpected behavior, and possible contract failures. Ensuring safe and atomic operations on class properties is crucial in maintaining the integrity and reliability of the smart contract.

# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Report: Bypassing `voteForNomineeWeights` Security Mechanisms

### Overview

This report highlights a critical vulnerability in the `voteForNomineeWeights` function of the `VoteWeighting` contract. The vulnerability stems from the lack of access control that persists well into the `addNomineeEVM` function, which is a critical piece in bypassing the intended security mechanisms of the `voteForNomineeWeights` function. This document provides a step-by-step explanation of how an attacker can exploit this vulnerability, the variables and logic that can be manipulated, and the state changes that will occur as a result.

### Affected Function
The primary function affected by this vulnerability is `voteForNomineeWeights`, which is designed to allow users to vote on the weights of different nominees.

### Links to Code
- `voteForNomineeWeights` function: [Link](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/governance/contracts/VoteWeighting.sol#L483)
- `addNomineeEVM` function: [Link](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/governance/contracts/VoteWeighting.sol#L324-L344)

### Step-by-Step Explanation of the Attack

1. **Exploiting the `addNomineeEVM` Function**:
   - **Public Access**: The `addNomineeEVM` function can be called by anyone.
   - **Lack of Access Control**: There are no restrictions on who can call this function, allowing any user to add a nominee.
   - **Adding Unauthorized Nominees**: An attacker can add nominees with arbitrary addresses and chain IDs, bypassing any intended restrictions on nominee additions.

2. **Setting Up for `voteForNomineeWeights`**:
   - **Initialize Parameters**: The attacker initializes parameters for the `voteForNomineeWeights` function with the unauthorized nominee added in the previous step.
   - **Construct Nominee Hash**: The `voteForNomineeWeights` function uses the `account` and `chainId` to create a nominee hash, which uniquely identifies the nominee.

3. **Voting for Nominee Weights**:
   - **Get User Voting Power**: The function retrieves the user's voting power and checks if the user has enough power to vote for the nominee's weight.
   - **Calculate New and Old Slopes**: The function calculates new and old slopes and biases based on the user's voting power and the nominee's current weight.
   - **Update Nominee Weight**: The function updates the nominee's weight based on the calculated slopes and biases.

4. **Potential Manipulations**:
   - **Manipulating Slope and Bias Calculations**: By adding unauthorized nominees, an attacker can manipulate the slope and bias calculations to favor their nominees.
   - **Vote Too Often**: The function checks if the user is voting too frequently. However, since the nominee is unauthorized, this check can be bypassed.
   - **Overflow Check**: The function checks if the new voting power exceeds the maximum allowed weight. An attacker can set a weight that bypasses this check.

5. **State Changes**:
   - **Persistent State Changes**: Once the unauthorized nominee is added, all state changes associated with this nominee persist. This includes changes to the `pointsWeight` mapping, which tracks the weight of each nominee.
   - **Impact on Nominee Weights**: Unauthorized nominees can significantly alter the weight distribution, affecting the overall voting process and the outcome of votes.

### Impact
- **Unauthorized Access**: The lack of access control allows any user to add nominees, compromising the integrity of the nomination process.
- **Manipulated Voting**: Unauthorized nominees can manipulate the voting process, affecting the distribution of weights and the outcome of votes.
- **Persistent State Changes**: Unauthorized state changes can persist, leading to long-term effects on the contract's state and behavior.

### Recommended Mitigations
To address these vulnerabilities, the following changes are recommended:

1. **Implement Access Control**:
   - Use access control mechanisms such as `onlyOwner` or role-based access controls to restrict who can call the `addNomineeEVM` function.

2. **Validate Nominee Existence**:
   - Ensure that nominees cannot be added multiple times or after being removed. Implement additional checks to validate the nominee's existence and eligibility.

3. **Re-evaluate Voting Mechanisms**:
   - Enhance the security checks within the `voteForNomineeWeights` function to ensure that unauthorized nominees cannot manipulate the voting process.

### Conclusion
This report highlights the critical vulnerability in the `voteForNomineeWeights` function, stemming from the lack of access control in the `addNomineeEVM` function. By implementing the recommended mitigations, the contract's security and integrity can be significantly improved, preventing unauthorized access and manipulation of the voting process.

## Vulnerability Report: Bypassing Checks and Manipulating Voting Power in `voteForNomineeWeights`

### Overview

This report identifies a vulnerability in the `voteForNomineeWeights` function of the `VoteWeighting` contract, where various checks are bypassed due to default zero values for unknown `msg.sender`. This allows an attacker to predict and manipulate the voting power, leading to unauthorized changes in nominee weights.

### Affected Function
The primary function affected by this vulnerability is `voteForNomineeWeights`.

### Links to Code
- `voteForNomineeWeights` function: [Link](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/governance/contracts/VoteWeighting.sol#L483)
- `getLastUserPoint` function: [Link](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/governance/contracts/veOLAS.sol#L145-L150)
- `lockedEnd` function: [Link](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/governance/contracts/veOLAS.sol#L153)

### Detailed Analysis

1. **Initialization of Variables for Unknown `msg.sender`**:
   - If `msg.sender` does not exist in the contract's mappings, functions like `getLastUserPoint` and `lockedEnd` return default zero values.
   - **`getLastUserPoint`**: Returns an uninitialized `PointVoting` struct, where `slope` and other fields are 0.
   - **`lockedEnd`**: Returns 0 if `msg.sender` has no locked balance.

2. **Predicting Power Used**:
   - **Old Slope and Bias**: For unknown `msg.sender`, `oldSlope` is uninitialized, resulting in `oldSlope.slope` and `oldSlope.end` being 0.
   - **New Slope and Bias**: Calculated as:
     ```solidity
     VotedSlope memory newSlope = VotedSlope({
         slope: uint256(uint128(userSlope)) * weight / MAX_WEIGHT,
         end: lockEnd,
         power: weight
     });
     ```
     Given `userSlope` and `lockEnd` are 0, `newSlope.slope` and `newSlope.end` are also 0. Hence, `newBias` becomes 0.
   - **Power Used**: 
     ```solidity
     uint256 powerUsed = voteUserPower[msg.sender];
     powerUsed = powerUsed + newSlope.power - oldSlope.power;
     voteUserPower[msg.sender] = powerUsed;
     ```
     Since both `newSlope.power` and `oldSlope.power` are 0 for unknown `msg.sender`, `powerUsed` equals `weight`.

3. **Bypassing Checks**:
   - **Weight Check**:
     ```solidity
     if (weight > MAX_WEIGHT) {
         revert Overflow(weight, MAX_WEIGHT);
     }
     ```
     This check ensures `weight` is within a valid range.
   - **Last Voting Time Check**:
     ```solidity
     uint256 nextAllowedVotingTime = lastUserVote[msg.sender][nomineeHash] + WEIGHT_VOTE_DELAY;
     if (nextAllowedVotingTime > block.timestamp) {
         revert VoteTooOften(msg.sender, block.timestamp, nextAllowedVotingTime);
     }
     ```
     For unknown `msg.sender`, `lastUserVote[msg.sender][nomineeHash]` is 0, making `nextAllowedVotingTime` equal to `WEIGHT_VOTE_DELAY`. Since this is significantly less than the current timestamp, the check is bypassed.

4. **State Changes**:
   - The unauthorized state changes persist, affecting the contract's state and behavior. For example:
     ```solidity
     pointsWeight[nomineeHash][nextTime].bias = _maxAndSub(_getWeight(account, chainId) + newBias, oldBias);
     ```
     Here, both `newBias` and `oldBias` are 0, so `pointsWeight[nomineeHash][nextTime].bias` is not altered significantly, but the unauthorized state change persists.

### Steps Taken by an Attacker

1. **Add Unauthorized Nominee**:
   - Using the public `addNomineeEVM` function, an attacker adds a nominee with arbitrary `account` and `chainId`.

2. **Prepare to Vote**:
   - The attacker initializes parameters for `voteForNomineeWeights` with the unauthorized nominee.

3. **Predict Power Used**:
   - The attacker predicts that `powerUsed` will equal the `weight` argument due to default zero values for unknown `msg.sender`.

4. **Bypass Checks**:
   - Bypass weight and last voting time checks due to known zero values for unknown `msg.sender`.

5. **Update State**:
   - Make unauthorized state changes that persist in the contract, affecting nominee weights and the overall voting process.

### Impact
- **Unauthorized Voting**: Allows an attacker to vote with predictable power, bypassing intended restrictions.
- **Persistent State Changes**: Unauthorized state changes persist, compromising the integrity of the contract.
- **Manipulated Voting Power**: An attacker can manipulate voting power to affect the outcome of votes and the distribution of weights.

### Recommended Mitigations

1. **Implement Access Control**:
   - Restrict access to critical functions like `addNomineeEVM` using `onlyOwner` or role-based access controls.

2. **Enhance Validation**:
   - Validate that `msg.sender` exists in the relevant mappings before proceeding with calculations and state changes.

3. **Re-evaluate Voting Mechanisms**:
   - Strengthen security checks within the `voteForNomineeWeights` function to prevent bypassing and unauthorized state changes.

### Conclusion
This report highlights how an attacker can exploit default zero values for unknown `msg.sender` to bypass checks and manipulate voting power in the `voteForNomineeWeights` function. By implementing the recommended mitigations, the contract's security and integrity can be significantly enhanced, preventing unauthorized access and manipulation of the voting process.

### Denial of Service (DoS) Potential
While the main issue is access control, the vulnerability also has a potential DoS component:

**Spam and Overload**: By allowing unauthorized additions and votes, an attacker can flood the system with bogus nominations or votes, potentially leading to a denial of service by overwhelming the system or causing it to reach its resource limits.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `getProxyAddressWithNonce` function currently utilizes a hardcoded prefix 0xff for address derivation, assuming Ethereum-like address conventions. This approach is vulnerable when deployed across multiple chains with differing address formats. Specifically:

Typical address aliasing in chains like Arbitrum or Optimism might break the assumption
of having the same prefix for different sub-accounts. Specifically, whenever an account is
a contract and not an externally owned account (EOA), Layer 1 to Layer 2 (L1 -> L2)
messages will have the msg.sender aliased with a mask. This might result in different
aliased account prefixes.

Chain-Specific Vulnerabilities:
Celo: Incorrect address format (0x followed by Base58Check) could lead to address generation failures.
Solana: Complete mismatch in address format (base58 encoding) renders the function unusable.

```javascript
function getProxyAddressWithNonce(address implementation, uint256 localNonce) public view returns (address) {
        // Get salt based on chain Id and nonce values
        bytes32 salt = keccak256(abi.encodePacked(block.chainid, localNonce));

        // Get the deployment data based on the proxy bytecode and the implementation address
        bytes memory deploymentData = abi.encodePacked(type(StakingProxy).creationCode,
            uint256(uint160(implementation)));

        // Get the hash forming the contract address
        bytes32 hash = keccak256(
            abi.encodePacked(
                bytes1(0xff), address(this), salt, keccak256(deploymentData)
            )
        );

        return address(uint160(uint256(hash)));
    }
```

Implement conditional logic or switch cases based on chain IDs to adjust prefix values (0xff for Ethereum, 0x8000 for zkSync Era, etc.).

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Using the >= operator for time comparisons against block.timestamp can introduce off-by-one errors due to the nature of how block.timestamp is updated only once per block. This can lead to unexpected behavior if the condition is met at the exact second when block.timestamp changes. This issue is especially critical in scenarios where time-sensitive operations are performed, potentially causing operations to revert unexpectedly or execute when they shouldn't.


## Proof of Concept
Consider the following code snippet:

```javascript
if (block.timestamp >= (_timeLaunch + ONE_YEAR)) {
    revert Overflow(_timeLaunch + ONE_YEAR, block.timestamp);
}
```
In this code, the condition checks if the current block.timestamp is greater than or equal to _timeLaunch + ONE_YEAR. If the condition is true, it reverts with an Overflow error.

In Solidity, using >= or <= to compare against block.timestamp (alias now) may introduce off-by-one errors due to the fact that block.timestamp is only updated once per block and its value remains constant throughout the block's execution. If an operation happens at the exact second when block.timestamp changes, it could result in unexpected behavior. To avoid this, it's safer to use strict inequality operators (> or <). For instance, if a condition should only be met after a certain time, use block.timestamp > time rather than block.timestamp >= time. This way, potential off-by-one errors due to the exact timing of block mining are mitigated, leading to safer, more predictable contract behavior.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

To avoid potential off-by-one errors, use strict inequality operators (> or <) instead of non-strict ones (>= or <=). This ensures that the condition only triggers after the specified time has completely passed.

```javascript
if (block.timestamp > (_timeLaunch + ONE_YEAR)) {
    revert Overflow(_timeLaunch + ONE_YEAR, block.timestamp);
}
```


## Assessed type

Math

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/main/registries/contracts/staking/StakingBase.sol#L407


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The use of staticcall in smart contracts, particularly when interacting with other contracts, poses a significant security risk. According to the solidity docs, if a staticcall encounters a state change, it burns up all gas and returns. If the called contract contains state-changing operations, it could potentially consume all available gas during the execution of the staticcall, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS) condition.

The `_checkRatioPass` function in the contract contains a vulnerability that could potentially lead to denial-of-service (DoS) attacks or out-of-gas errors. This vulnerability arises due to the use of staticcall without limiting the amount of gas forwarded, which could result in the exhaustion of all available gas if the called function attempts to modify state.

This vulnerability has already been called out in known protocols ie balancer and has been addressed see below

https://github.com/balancer/balancer-v2-monorepo/blob/227683919a7031615c0bc7f144666cdf3883d212/pkg/pool-utils/contracts/lib/VaultReentrancyLib.sol#L48-L53

According to EIP150, a call gets allocated 63/64 bits of the gas, and the entire 63/64 parts of the gas is burnt up after the staticcall, since the staticcall will always encounter a storage change.

Similar Finding https://solodit.xyz/issues/m-17-oog-unexpected-reverts-due-to-incorrect-usage-of-staticcall-sherlock-tokemak-git

## Proof of Concept

Consider a smart contract that uses staticcall to interact with another contract, which, upon interaction, performs state-changing operations. If the called contract's operations are not properly bounded or if the gas limit for the staticcall is not adequately capped, the entire gas budget allocated for the transaction could be consumed by the called contract's operations. This could lead to a situation where subsequent operations within the same transaction fail due to insufficient gas, effectively causing a DoS condition.

An attacker crafts a malicious signature and sends a transaction invoking the `_checkRatioPass` function with excessive gas. The `_checkRatioPass` function executes a staticcall to the signer's address to validate the signature. If the called function within the signer contract performs any state-changing operations, it consumes all available gas, leading to an out-of-gas error. As a result, the transaction fails, potentially causing a denial-of-service condition.


## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
modify the `_checkRatioPass` function to include a fixed gas stipend when performing the staticcall. This ensures that even if the called function attempts to change state, it won't consume excessive gas or cause out-of-gas errors.

```javascript
(bool success, bytes memory returnData) = activityChecker.staticcall{gas: FIXED_GAS_AMOUNT}(activityData);
```


## Assessed type

DoS

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The current condition for checking if a nominee already exists or has been removed uses a logical AND (`&&`) operator. This logic fails to accurately determine the presence of a nominee in the active or removed lists, potentially allowing duplicate entries or blocking valid ones. This issue can lead to inconsistencies in the contract's state and mismanagement of nominees, which can affect the integrity and reliability of the voting system.

## Proof of Concept
The incorrect condition is located in the `_addNominee` function:
```solidity
if (mapRemovedNominees[nomineeHash] > 0 && mapNomineeIds[nomineeHash] > 0) {
    revert NomineeAlreadyExists(nominee.account, nominee.chainId);
}
```
This should use a logical OR (`||`) instead of a logical AND (`&&`).

The corrected condition should be:
```solidity
if (mapRemovedNominees[nomineeHash] > 0 || mapNomineeIds[nomineeHash] > 0) {
    revert NomineeAlreadyExists(nominee.account, nominee.chainId);
}
```

If you attempt to add a nominee that exists in either the active or removed list, the contract will not correctly revert, potentially allowing duplicates. Conversely, valid nominees might be incorrectly rejected.

## Tools Used
Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Update the condition in the `_addNominee` function to use a logical OR (`||`) instead of a logical AND (`&&`). This ensures that the check correctly identifies if a nominee is already present in either the active or removed lists.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/registries/contracts/staking/StakingBase.sol#L411


# Vulnerability details

The `_checkRatioPass` function is critical for maintaining the integrity and security of a staking mechanism by verifying the activity of a service through nonce comparison over time. This function checks the liveness of a multisig address by comparing the current nonces with the last recorded nonces over a given time span (`ts`). 

The current implementation uses the condition `returnData.length > 63`, which is incorrect and potentially harmful. This check is supposed to ensure that the returned data contains at least two nonces, which is necessary for a meaningful comparison. However, the condition `returnData.length > 63` is not sufficient to guarantee this.

## POC

1. **ABI Encoding Standards**:
   - According to the ABI encoding rules, the dynamic array encoding consists of a 32-byte length prefix followed by the array elements.
   - For an array with two nonces, the encoded data length should be:
     \[
     \text{Length field (32 bytes)} + \text{Nonce 1 (32 bytes)} + \text{Nonce 2 (32 bytes)} = 96 \text{ bytes}
     \]

2. **Impact of the Incorrect Check**:
   - If the length check is set to `returnData.length > 63`, it only ensures the presence of one nonce (32 bytes length field + 32 bytes for one nonce).
   - This could result in situations where only one nonce is available, making it impossible to perform a valid comparison of activity levels.
   - Without at least two nonces, the function cannot accurately measure the change in nonce values over time, rendering the liveness check ineffective.
   - This can lead to incorrect determinations about the service's activity, potentially affecting the integrity of the staking mechanism.

## Impact
- **Security and Integrity Risks**:
  - By not properly verifying the presence of at least two nonces, the staking mechanism may fail to detect inactivity or insufficient activity levels of the multisig.
  - This compromises the liveness checks, which are critical for ensuring that services are actively participating and not just occupying staking slots without genuine activity.

- **Operational Issues**:
  - Services that should be flagged for inactivity may continue to be considered active, receiving rewards or maintaining their staked status without meeting the required activity criteria.
  - This miscalculation could affect the distribution of rewards and the overall fairness of the staking system.


## Tools Used
Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

The correct check should ensure that the return data contains at least 96 bytes, which accounts for the 32-byte length field and two 32-byte nonces. Therefore, the condition should be updated to:

```solidity
if (success && returnData.length >= 96 && (returnData.length % 32 == 0)) {
    // Parse nonces
    currentNonces = abi.decode(returnData, (uint256[]));

    // Get the ratio pass activity check
    activityData = abi.encodeCall(IActivityChecker.isRatioPass, (currentNonces, lastNonces, ts));
    (success, returnData) = activityChecker.staticcall(activityData);

    // The return data must match the size of bool
    if (success && returnData.length == 32) {
        ratioPass = abi.decode(returnData, (bool));
    }
}
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/main/governance/contracts/VoteWeighting.sol#L532
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/main/governance/contracts/VoteWeighting.sol#L578


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The current implementation of the `_maxAndSub` function in the `VoteWeighting` contract can lead to incorrect updates of nominee weights and the total weight sum. Specifically, when the `oldBias` value is greater than the sum of the current weight (`_getWeight(account, chainId)`) and the new bias (`newBias`), or greater than the sum of the current total weight (`_getSum()`) and the new bias, the `_maxAndSub` function silently returns 0. This behavior can result in the following impacts:

1. **Inaccurate Weight History**: Incorrect historical data for nominee weights, making it difficult to track and audit past voting behavior accurately.
2. **Misrepresentation of Voting Power**: Nominees whose weights are incorrectly set to zero may lose their voting power, misrepresenting the actual distribution of voting power.
3. **Disproportionate Influence**: Other nominees might gain disproportionate influence if certain nominees' weights are set to zero, disrupting the intended balance of power and fairness in the voting process.
4. **Silent Failure**: The function silently fails without providing any indication or error message, making it challenging to detect and debug issues.
5. **Risk of Manipulation**: Malicious actors could exploit this behavior to manipulate the voting system by deliberately causing underflows to zero out weights and sums, thereby altering the voting dynamics to their advantage or detriment of everyone.

## Proof of Concept

### Line of Code
```solidity
function _maxAndSub(uint256 a, uint256 b) internal pure returns (uint256) {
    return a > b ? a - b : 0;
}
```

### Affected Code Snippet

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/main/governance/contracts/VoteWeighting.sol#L532

1. Updating nominee weights:
```solidity
pointsWeight[nomineeHash][nextTime].bias = _maxAndSub(_getWeight(account, chainId) + newBias, oldBias);
```

2. Updating total weight sum:
```solidity
pointsSum[nextTime].bias = _maxAndSub(_getSum() + newBias, oldBias);
```

### Example Scenario

1. **Inaccurate Weight History**:
   - Suppose a nominee had a weight of 1000 (`oldBias = 1000 * time difference`). After some votes, the new weight calculation results in a combined weight of 500 (current weight + new bias). Since 1000 > 500, the `_maxAndSub` function sets the weight to zero, inaccurately recording the nominee's weight as zero.

2. **Misrepresentation of Voting Power**:
   - A user votes for a nominee, initially giving them a weight of 800 (`oldBias = 800 * time difference`). Later, the user's voting power decreases, and the new calculation results in a combined weight of 400. Since 800 > 400, the weight is set to zero, misrepresenting the nominee's actual voting power.
   
3. **Disproportionate Influence**: 
   - Nominee A has a significant weight of 1500. After an underflow due to a new vote, their weight is set to zero. Other nominees with stable weights (e.g., 600, 700) now have disproportionate influence compared to their intended distribution.

4. **Silent Failure**: 

   - During a routine update, the system recalculates weights. Due to an unexpected change, the oldBias is greater than the combined weight, setting the value to zero without any error message. The failure goes unnoticed, leading to inaccurate governance data.


## Tools Used

Manual code review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Replace the `_maxAndSub` function with a safe subtraction function that reverts the transaction when an underflow occurs. Here's an example implementation:

```solidity
function _safeSub(uint256 a, uint256 b) internal pure returns (uint256) {
    require(b <= a, "Subtraction overflow");
    return a - b;
}
```

### Update Affected Code Snippets

1. Updating nominee weights:
```solidity
pointsWeight[nomineeHash][nextTime].bias = _safeSub(_getWeight(account, chainId) + newBias, oldBias);
```

2. Updating total weight sum:
```solidity
pointsSum[nextTime].bias = _safeSub(_getSum() + newBias, oldBias);
```

By using the `_safeSub` function, if `oldBias` is greater than `_getWeight(account, chainId) + newBias` or `_getSum() + newBias`, the transaction will revert with an explicit error message, preventing incorrect state updates and alerting the contract administrators to potential issues.



## Assessed type

Under/Overflow

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/registries/contracts/staking/StakingFactory.sol#L150-L154


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
According to the Ethereum contract address generation scheme, the correct order of parameters should be:
```solidity
keccak256(0xff ++ address(this) ++ salt ++ keccak256(init_code))[12:]
```
However, in the getProxyAddressWithNonce code, the order of parameters is incorrect: [@StakingFactory.sol:150-154](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/registries/contracts/staking/StakingFactory.sol#L150-L154)
```solidity
bytes32 hash = keccak256(
    abi.encodePacked(
        bytes1(0xff), address(this), salt, keccak256(deploymentData)
    )
);
```
The `salt` and `keccak256(deploymentData)` are in the wrong order. The correct order should be:
```solidity
bytes32 hash = keccak256(
    abi.encodePacked(
        bytes1(0xff), address(this), keccak256(deploymentData), salt
    )
);
```
This bug will result in incorrect proxy addresses being calculated, which can lead to unexpected behavior and potential vulnerabilities.

## Proof of Concept
Refer to the Ethereum contract address generation scheme, which is documented in the Ethereum Yellow Paper https://ethereum.github.io/yellowpaper/paper.pdf in section 7.2 "Contract Creation" and Appendix F "Signing Transactions".

The Ethereum Yellow Paper clearly specifies the order of parameters for contract address generation:
```solidity
keccak256(0xff ++ address(this) ++ salt ++ keccak256(init_code))[12:]
```
This further validates that the order of parameters in the provided code is incorrect.

The bug in the `getProxyAddressWithNonce` can lead to incorrect proxy address calculations, unintended contract interactions, increased collision risks, and difficulties in contract verification.

## Tools Used
Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The correct order of parameters should be.
```solidity
bytes32 hash = keccak256(
    abi.encodePacked(
        bytes1(0xff), address(this), keccak256(deploymentData), salt
    )
);
```

# Vulnerability details

_sendMessage function checks for the `maxSubmissionCostToken` and `maxSubmissionCostMessage` parameters to be non-zero before proceeding with the transfer. However, if these values are zero, the function will revert with a `ZeroValue` error.

This is because the `maxSubmissionCostToken` and `maxSubmissionCostMessage` parameters are used in the calculation of the total cost of the message transfer, which is then compared to the value of `msg.value`. If either of these values is zero, the function will revert with a `LowerThan` error if the total cost exceeds the value of `msg.value`.

However, if the `maxSubmissionCostToken` and `maxSubmissionCostMessage` parameters are both zero, the function will not proceed with the transfer and will instead revert with a `ZeroValue` error. This is because the calculation of the total cost will result in a value that is greater than or equal to the value of `msg.value`, which will cause the `LowerThan` error to be thrown.

## Impact
The reason for this is that the function uses these parameters in the calculation of the total cost of the message transfer, which is then compared to the value of `msg.value`. If either of these values is zero, the function will revert with a `LowerThan` error if the total cost exceeds the value of `msg.value`.

However, if both the `maxSubmissionCostToken` and `maxSubmissionCostMessage` parameters are zero, the function will not proceed with the transfer and will instead revert with a `ZeroValue` error. This is because the calculation of the total cost will result in a value that is greater than or equal to the value of `msg.value`, which will cause the `LowerThan` error to be thrown.

[@ArbitrumDepositProcessorL1.sol:111-192](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/tokenomics/contracts/staking/ArbitrumDepositProcessorL1.sol#L119-L192)
