# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/registries/contracts/staking/StakingBase.sol#L818-L820


# Vulnerability details

Relevant code: [StakingBase::unstake](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/registries/contracts/staking/StakingBase.sol#L818-L820)

### Description
The `Staking` contract is designed to make sure a service can be unstaked only under certain conditions. This is done to prevent exploitative actions like staking and unstaking as soon as possible after rewards are distributed.

Inside the `unstake` function, one such preventative check ensures a service can't be unstaked before the minimum duration, when the `Staking` contract has rewards:
```javascript
if (ts <= minStakingDuration && availableRewards > 0) {
    revert NotEnoughTimeStaked(serviceId, ts, minStakingDuration);
}
```

This mechanism can be gamed by malicious actors who can deposit **dust** amounts in the `Staking` contract and unfairly prevent services from unstaking. This has the unintended consequence of keeping services in an essentially empty `Staking` contract.

Deposit functions in `StakingToken` and `StakingNativeToken` respectively
```javascript
function deposit(uint256 amount) external {
	uint256 newBalance = balance + amount;
	uint256 newAvailableRewards = availableRewards + amount;
	...
}
```
&
```javascript
receive() external payable {
	uint256 newBalance = balance + msg.value;
	uint256 newAvailableRewards = availableRewards + msg.value;
	...
}
```
Have no checks for minimum deposit amount, making this attack really cheap. Because of the comparison to 0, `availableRewards` can be as small as 1 wei.

### Root Cause
Dust rewards prevent unstaking before minimum duration has passed.
### Impact
A service can be kept in an unfavourable `Staking` contract. This causes opportunity loss for the owner, because they could `stake` in another contract during this time. Service owners can keep the competition locked in another staking contract.

### PoC
Imagine the following scenario:
- **5 services** are in a `Staking` contract with long min duration.
- A **6th** one joins.
- Another `Staking` contract is instantiated with more favourable rewards.
- All **5 services** unstake without any issues.
- Just after that, someone **deposits dust** amounts in the `Staking` contract to reduce the competition in the newer `Staking` contract.
- **Service #6** now has to either - wait for the next checkpoint, collect rewards and try to unstake, or wait the whole min stake duration and then unstake.

In the worst case scenario, multiple services are left in the `Staking` contract and a malicious actor **deposits dust** after each `checkpoint()` call, forcing them to wait the minimum stake duration.

### Suggested Mitigation
Unfortunately, the only way to completely prevent abusing this mechanism is to remove the `availableRewards > 0` check and make all services wait for the minimum duration. This would not be ideal, but at least the opportunity loss potential would be equal to all.

A more precise solution would be to add an additional `StakingParam` that would control the right-hand side of the check: 
```javascript
if (ts <= minStakingDuration && availableRewards > minStakingFunds) { ... }
```
In this way, such an attack can be a lot more costlier and will disincentivize it.

It would also help to **prevent deposit of dust amounts** in the corresponding `Staking` contracts.


## Assessed type

DoS

# Vulnerability details

Relevant code: [StakingBase::unstake](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/registries/contracts/staking/StakingBase.sol#L867-L869), [StakingToken::\_withdraw](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/registries/contracts/staking/StakingToken.sol#L104-L111), [StakingNativeToken::\_withdraw](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/registries/contracts/staking/StakingNativeToken.sol#L28-L37) 
### Description
Upon calling the `unstake` function, it ensures that the unstaking service collects any pending rewards:
```javascript
if (reward > 0) {
    _withdraw(multisig, reward);
}
```
The withdraw implementation is different, depending on wether the `Staking` contract distributes tokens or native currency as rewards, but it essentially boils down to subtracting rewards from the current balance and transferring them to the service multisig - `balance -= amount;`. 

The mandatory collection of reward can cause the service to be staked for much longer than it's owner intended to. Consider a situation where the `Staking` contract has no funds to distribute and all calls to `unstake` revert due to an underflow in the `_withdraw` function: `balance -= amount;`. 

### Root Cause
Lack of force unstake mechanism that will forfeit rewards in favour of the service owner being able to stake elsewhere.

### Impact
Having a `Staking` contract without funds to distribute can be especially damaging in cases where there are multiple services staked with pending rewards. In such situations owners will either have to wait for new rewards without any guarantees of new funds arriving or they would have to deposit themselves so they can unstake. The second option puts their funds at risk, as another service could use their deposit to unstake before them.

The lack of **force unstake** creates a peculiar situation where service owners could incur opportunity loss or have to potentially pay to unstake (with the risk of losing funds). 

### PoC
Lets suppose the following turn of events:
- `Staking` contract stops receiving regular funding
- Services have rewards pending that are more than the current `balance` in the contract.
- Service owners can't unstake and move to a more profitable `Staking` contract.
- If a service owner deposits in the `Staking` contract themselves, they could get frontrun by another owner and lose their funds.

### Suggested Mitigation
Add a `forceUnstake` flag that will allow `unstake` without receiving the pending rewards. It could look something like this:
```javascript
if (forceUnstake) {
	sInfo.reward = 0;
	reward = 0;
} else if (reward > 0) {
	_withdraw(multisig, reward);
}
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/tokenomics/contracts/staking/ArbitrumDepositProcessorL1.sol#L134-L137


# Vulnerability details

Relevant code: [ArbitrumDepositProcessorL1::\_sendMessage](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/tokenomics/contracts/staking/ArbitrumDepositProcessorL1.sol#L134-L137)
### Description
The `Dispenser` contract is responsible for distributing token incentives across `Staking` contracts deployed on various blockchains. Every chain has a corresponding `depositProcessor` contract, which facilitates the bridging and handles chain-specific transfers/messaging:
```javascript
address stakingTargetEVM = address(uint160(uint256(stakingTarget)));
IDepositProcessor(depositProcessor).sendMessage{value:msg.value}(stakingTargetEVM, stakingIncentive,
        bridgePayload, transferAmount);
```

In every `IDepositProcessor`, the only contract able to call `sendMessage` is the `Dispenser`:
```javascript
if (msg.sender != l1Dispenser) {
	revert ManagerOnly(l1Dispenser, msg.sender);
}
```

When bridging funds to Arbitrum, one of the parameters encoded in the `bridgePayload` is `refundAccount`. This refund address is going to receive all of the excess gas that was sent during bridging. Here's the Arbitrum natspec about the bridging function:
```javascript
/**
 * @notice Deposit ERC20 token from Ethereum into Arbitrum. If L2 side hasn't been deployed yet, includes name/symbol/decimals data for initial L2 deploy. Initiate by GatewayRouter.
 * @dev L2 address alias will not be applied to the following types of addresses on L1:
 *      - an externally-owned account
 *      - a contract in construction
 *      - an address where a contract will be created
 *      - an address where a contract lived, but was destroyed
 * @param _l1Token L1 address of ERC20
 * @param _refundTo Account, or its L2 alias if it have code in L1, to be credited with excess gas refund in L2
 * @param _to Account to be credited with the tokens in the L2 (can be the user's L2 account or a contract), not subject to L2 aliasing
              This account, or its L2 alias if it have code in L1, will also be able to cancel the retryable ticket and receive callvalue refund
 * @param _amount Token Amount
 * @param _maxGas Max gas deducted from user's L2 balance to cover L2 execution
 * @param _gasPriceBid Gas price for L2 execution
 * @param _data encoded data from router and user
 * @return res abi encoded inbox sequence number
 */
//  * @param maxSubmissionCost Max gas deducted from user's L2 balance to cover base submission fee
function outboundTransferCustomRefund(
    address _l1Token,
    address _refundTo,
    address _to,
    uint256 _amount,
    uint256 _maxGas,
    uint256 _gasPriceBid,
    bytes calldata _data
) public payable virtual override returns (bytes memory res)
```


In case such address is not given in the payload, a default address is set by the `ArbitrumDepositProcessorL1`:
```javascript
// If refundAccount is zero, default to msg.sender
if (refundAccount == address(0)) {
    refundAccount = msg.sender;
}
```

The issue with `Dispenser` being the `refundAccount` is that the gas refund needs to be done from the L2 side and `Dispenser` is unable to use it.

### Root Cause
Refunds from excess gas are sent to L2 aliased address without any way to use them.

### Impact
Gas refunds are lost when `refundAccount == Dispenser`. Thus, the contract would lose value under certain conditions. In a protocol which depends on bridging tokens, therefore paying gas fees regularly, these refunds will accrue to a substantial amount over time.

### Suggested Mitigation
The default refund address should be configurable and deployed on L2. The best candidate would be `ArbitrumTargetDispenserL2`.


## Assessed type

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/tokenomics/contracts/staking/WormholeDepositProcessorL1.sol#L96-L97


# Vulnerability details

Relevant code: [WormholeDepositProcessorL1::\_sendMessage](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/tokenomics/contracts/staking/WormholeDepositProcessorL1.sol#L96-L97) 
### Description
The deposit processors used for bridging on L1 work in 2 possible ways:
- They can send tokens
- Or send a message to L2 (in case of enough withheld tokens)

Some examples are `GnosisDepositProcessorL1::_sendMessage`:
```javascript
if (transferAmount > 0) {
	...
    bytes memory data = abi.encode(targets, stakingIncentives);
    IBridge(l1TokenRelayer).relayTokensAndCall(olas, l2TargetDispenser, transferAmount, data); 
    ...
} else {
	...
    bytes32 iMsg = IBridge(l1MessageRelayer).requireToPassMessage(l2TargetDispenser, data, gasLimitMessage);
    ...
}
```

`ArbitrumDepositProcessorL1::_sendMessage`:
```javascript
if (transferAmount > 0) {
	...
    IBridge(l1TokenRelayer).outboundTransferCustomRefund{value: cost[0]}(olas, refundAccount,
        l2TargetDispenser, transferAmount, TOKEN_GAS_LIMIT, gasPriceBid, submissionCostData);
}
...
sequence = IBridge(l1MessageRelayer).createRetryableTicket{value: cost[1]}(l2TargetDispenser, 0,
    maxSubmissionCostMessage, refundAccount, refundAccount, gasLimitMessage, gasPriceBid, data);
```

The same is true for `Optimism` and `Polygon` processors as well.

The only deposit processor that is not implemented like this is `WormholeDepositProcessorL1`. This means that every time we might want to only send a message, the token bridging flow will be triggered, which wastes additional resources on every call.

The other issue is that according to the Readme, one of the chains **Olas** is going to be deployed to is **Solana**. `WormholeDepositProcessorL1` is the only way to send messages/tokens to the **Solana** chain. Thus, it should use the [corresponding](https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/wormhole-solidity-sdk/blob/b9e129e65d34827d92fceeed8c87d3ecdfc801d0/src/TokenBase.sol#L52-L65) `transferTokens` function when `wormholeTargetChainId` points to a [non-evm chain](https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/wormhole-solidity-sdk/blob/main/src/Chains.sol).
### Root Cause
1. Using token bridging when a simple cross-chain message is enough. The following function is always called:
```javascript
sequence = sendTokenWithPayloadToEvm(uint16(wormholeTargetChainId), l2TargetDispenser, data, 0, gasLimitMessage, olas, transferAmount, uint16(l2TargetChainId), refundAccount);
```
2. Always making function call for `EVM`-based chain, even though its possible that `wormholeTargetChainId == 1` [(Solana)](https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/wormhole-solidity-sdk/blob/main/src/Chains.sol) 
### Impact
Users claiming fees for `Staking` contracts are forced to always use the token bridging flow and pay higher transaction fees than necessary. Over time overpaying in fees will sum up to a sizeable amount, especially considering the high dependency on cross-chain transactions.

`WormholeDepositProcessorL1` does not work with non-EVM functions, even though it is planned to do so. This can cause loss of funds when distributing token incentives.

### Suggested Mitigation
The `l1MessageRelayer` is able to send messages to EVM and non-EVM chains via [sendPayloadToEvm](https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/wormhole/blob/305cb8f0fe5fb349e243da73b619bcba39676e25/relayer/ethereum/contracts/interfaces/relayer/IWormholeRelayer.sol#L114-L122) and [send](https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/wormhole/blob/305cb8f0fe5fb349e243da73b619bcba39676e25/relayer/ethereum/contracts/interfaces/relayer/IWormholeRelayer.sol#L300-L312) respectively when `transferAmount == 0`.

Use [transferTokens](https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/wormhole-solidity-sdk/blob/b9e129e65d34827d92fceeed8c87d3ecdfc801d0/src/TokenBase.sol#L52-L65) function call when bridging tokens to non-EVM chains.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/governance/contracts/VoteWeighting.sol#L605
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/governance/contracts/VoteWeighting.sol#L605
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/governance/contracts/VoteWeighting.sol#L489


# Vulnerability details

## Description
There is a rounding error in the `nextTime` calculation due to dividing before multiplying by `WEEK`:
```solidity
uint256 nextTime = (block.timestamp + WEEK) / WEEK * WEEK;
```

The calculation of `nextTime` using integer division rounds down the result. When `block.timestamp + WEEK` is divided by `WEEK` before multiplying by `WEEK`, it causes the intermediate division result to round down, leading to an incorrect `nextTime`.
## Impact
- The incorrect `nextTime` value results in an inaccurate lock period.
- Users may vote after their lock period has expired, compromising the integrity of the voting system.
## Proof of Concept
Assuming:
- `block.timestamp = NOW`
- `WEEK = 86400 * 7` (one week in seconds)

Given:
- `NOW = 1622520000` (an example timestamp)
- `WEEK = 604800` seconds

Current calculation:
`uint256 nextTime = (1622520000 + 604800) / 604800 * 604800; // nextTime = 1623124800 / 604800 * 604800 = 2681 * 604800 = 1622524800`

Expected `nextTime`:
`1622520000 + 604800 = 1623124800`

The error is `1623124800 - 1622524800 = 4800` seconds (1 hour 20 minutes).

## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Change the calculation to multiply by `WEEK` first, then divide by `WEEK`:
uint256 nextTime = (block.timestamp + WEEK) * WEEK / WEEK;


## Assessed type

Math

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/registries/contracts/staking/StakingVerifier.sol#L193
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/registries/contracts/staking/StakingVerifier.sol#L244
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/registries/contracts/staking/StakingBase.sol#L317


# Vulnerability details

## Description
When executing the deposit internal function at the EthereumDepositProcessor contract, the contract calls StakingFactory.verifyInstanceAndGetEmissionsAmount to check the validity of parameters.
In this context, the verifyInstance function at the StakingVerifier contract checks if the instance receiving the deposit has its rewardsPerSecond within acceptable bounds otherwise it reverts the call by returning the false boolean:
```solidity
function verifyInstance(address instance, address implementation) external view returns (bool) {
        ...
        // Check for the staking parameters
        // This is a must have parameter for all staking contracts
        uint256 rewardsPerSecond = IStaking(instance).rewardsPerSecond();
        if (rewardsPerSecond > rewardsPerSecondLimit) {
            return false;
        }
        ...
}    
```

The changeStakingLimits function at the StakingVerifier contract allows the owner to arbitrarily change the rewardsPerSecondLimit public uint256 without checking if this breaks the integration with any staking instance.
This can lead to staking instances not being able to receive deposits after the limits are altered.

## Impact
Some staking instances may lose their ability to receive deposits due to a non-sanity-checked admin function.
Even though the function is admin-controlled, the issue is a case of unintended side-effects of an admin function that lead to the bricking of a contract's functionality.
As a staking instance's rewardsPerSecond variable is only able to be altered during the initialization of the StakingBase contract, this admin action renders the staking instances unable to receive deposits till the admin changes back the rewards per second limit.
This can lead to the loss of services as their staking instances have to be redeployed from scratch.

## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Ensure changes in reward limits are properly communicated and have enough time for services to adapt beforehand.
An option to reduce the impact of changeStakingLimits calls would be to add a function for staking contract owners to change their rewardsPerSecond after its initialization.

The migrate function at the DefaultTargetDispenserL2 contract migrates funds to a new specified L2 target dispenser contract address. It also removes the owner of the contract and makes it useless as it transfers away all its OLAS balance - therefore staking incentives cannot be redeemed.

The issue with that is that even though L2 Dispenser contracts may already have been migrated, nothing stops receiveMessage calls from being done. In the specific case in which the messageRelayer relays a received message right after the contract owner has called migrate, the 
processData internal function will add the staking incentives to the stakingQueueingNonces mapping-based queue but it cannot ever be redeemed. 

To make matters worse, the migrate function doesn't ensure the previously queued staking incentives are processed or migrated.
## Impact
Previously queued staking incentives are not sent nor migrated to their targets.
Messages relayed after a migrate function call may never be redeemed either.

Severity is high as it leads to the loss of whole incentives.
Likelihood is medium as staking queues are expected to have pending incentives.
## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Ensure the stakingQueueingNonces is fully paid or fully added to the new dispenser before removing OLAS funds from the contract.
Make sure the contract is not allowed to receive messages once its paused and/or has no owner - as it signals the migration has been completed.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/governance/contracts/VoteWeighting.sol#L159
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/tokenomics/contracts/Dispenser.sol#L275


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The OLAS protocol incorrectly assumes that the maximum `CHAIN_ID` value is `type(uint64).max / 2 - 36`, based on a misinterpretation of EVM specifications. The EVM specification, however, does not enforce such an upper bound limit for `CHAIN_ID`, which is defined as an unsigned 256-bit number.

Although EIP-2294 proposed an upper bound limit of `type(uint64).max / 2 - 36`, it is not in a Final state and has been stagnant for over two and a half years. Consequently, there is no standardized maximum value for `CHAIN_ID`, and a network could theoretically use a `CHAIN_ID` greater than `type(uint64).max / 2 - 36`, making it incompatible with the OLAS protocol.

While the likelihood of this issue occurring is low, its potential impact is significant, warranting a medium severity rating.

## Proof of Concept

The issue arises from the following incorrect assumption in the OLAS protocol:

```sol
// Maximum chain Id as per EVM specs
uint256 public constant MAX_EVM_CHAIN_ID = type(uint64).max / 2 - 36;
```

This line of code would fail for any `CHAIN_ID` that exceeds the assumed maximum value. However, the EVM allows `CHAIN_ID` to be any unsigned 256-bit integer, leading to a potential lack of support for such a network.

For further reference, the EVMC (Ethereum Client) which implements the EVM specification confirms that `CHAIN_ID` is an unsigned 256-bit number:

https://github.com/ethereum/evmc/blob/613889ba0b92abec2fbca861eb3958cb6af68ca4/include/evmc/evmc.h#L222

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Remove the assumption of a maximum `CHAIN_ID` value based on EIP-2294. Ensure the OLAS protocol can handle any valid `uint256` value for `CHAIN_ID`.


## Assessed type

Error

Consequently, any NFT sent to these contracts is irrecoverably lost, leading to potential loss of valuable assets and user funds.

The vulnerability can be verified by reviewing the inheritance structure and the absence of NFT management functions within the `StakingBase`, `StakingNativeToken`, and `StakingToken` contracts:

- `StakingBase` inherits from Solmate's `ERC721TokenReceiver`, which means it is designed to receive NFTs.
- There are no functions implemented in `StakingBase`, `StakingNativeToken`, or `StakingToken` to manage, transfer, or withdraw NFTs.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/main/tokenomics/contracts/Dispenser.sol?plain=1#L573


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The front-running vulnerability discovered in the ``claimStakingIncentivesBatch`` function of the Dispenser contract allows an attacker to exploit transaction ordering to manipulate state changes and transaction outcomes. By preempting transactions, an attacker could potentially alter the sequence of critical operations. Legitimate users claiming staking incentives might receive less than expected due to the attacker's manipulation.Attackers can exploit the vulnerability to gain a larger share of staking rewards, undermining the fairness of the system. 
## Proof of Concept
The provided test rule highlights the potential for a front-running vulnerability in the ``claimStakingIncentivesBatch`` function by simulating two transactions and analysing their outcomes.

Understanding the Code Snippet:
f(e1, arg): This represents a call to the function ``claimStakingIncentivesBatch()`` within a specific environment (e1) with arguments (arg).
!lastReverted: This checks if the previous call to f did not revert (meaning it was successful).
env e2; calldata arg2: These lines define a new environment (e2) and arguments (arg2) for a second call to f.
require e2.msg.sender != e1.msg.sender: This ensures the sender addresses for the two calls (f(e1, arg) and f(e2, arg2)) are different, likely simulating two separate users.
f(e2, arg2) at initialStorage: This calls f again in the e2 environment with arg2 arguments, but crucially, it uses initialStorage. This suggests the attacker might be trying to exploit the initial state of the contract before the first call modifies it.
f@withrevert(e1, arg): This calls f again in the e1 environment with arg arguments, but with a @withrevert decorator, indicating it's expected to revert.
!lastReverted: This checks if the last call to f reverted (as expected).
assert succeeded: This assertion fails because succeeded is set to !lastReverted, which would be false if the expected revert in the previous call didn't happen.
```solidity
f(e1, arg); 
	bool firstSucceeded = !lastReverted;
	env e2;
	calldataarg arg2;
	require e2.msg.sender != e1.msg.sender;
	f(e2, arg2) at initialStorage; 
	f@withrevert(e1, arg);
	bool succeeded = !lastReverted;
	assert succeeded
```
How it Reveals Frontrunning:
Initial Call (f(e1, arg)): The first call to f (presumably by a legitimate user) might have reverted due to various reasons (e.g., insufficient balance, exceeding claim limits).
Exploiting Initial State (f(e2, arg2) at initialStorage): The second call (f(e2, arg2)) in a different environment (e2) attempts to exploit the initial state (before the first call's modifications). This suggests the attacker might be trying to manipulate calculations or checks that rely on storage variables in their original state.
Second Call Outcome Uncertain: The outcome of this second call with initialStorage is unclear. However, the attacker might be hoping to gain an advantage based on the initial state, potentially leading to the first call receiving less than intended or failing altogether.
```solidity
Assert message: succeeded - Benchmarking.spec line 56
Violated for: 
claimStakingIncentives(uint256,uint256,bytes32,bytes),
claimStakingIncentivesBatch(uint256,uint256[],bytes32[][],bytes[],uint256[]),
calculateStakingIncentives(uint256,uint256,bytes32,uint256),
retain(),
claimOwnerIncentives(uint256[],uint256[])
```
The test output confirms that an attacker could potentially exploit these functions to gain an unfair advantage through front-running tactics.
## Tools Used
Formal verification
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Exploring the use of commit-reveal schemes or verifiable random functions (VRFs) if applicable.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/main/tokenomics/contracts/Dispenser.sol?plain=1#L849


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The identified vulnerability lies within the ``claimStakingIncentives`` function of the Dispenser contract. This function allows users to claim staking incentives based on certain parameters such as the number of claimed epochs, chain ID, staking target, and bridge payload. The vulnerability stems from the possibility of exploiting the function to perform actions that were not intended by the original design, potentially leading to unauthorized benefits or disruptions in the staking process.

## Proof of Concept
Ran tests using formal verification:
```CVL2
require e1.msg.sender!= e2.msg.sender;

    storage init = lastStorage;

    // Client's attempt to claim staking incentives
    claimStakingIncentives(e1, numClaimedEpochsClient, chainIdClient, stakingTargetClient, bridgePayloadClient); // if pass not reverted
    
    // Attacker's attempt to claim staking incentives
    claimStakingIncentives(e2, numClaimedEpochsAttacker, chainIdAttacker, stakingTargetAttacker, bridgePayloadAttacker) at init; // attacker attack

    // Attempt to claim staking incentives with the same parameters as the client
    claimStakingIncentives@withrevert(e1, numClaimedEpochsClient, chainIdClient, stakingTargetClient, bridgePayloadClient);

    assert!lastReverted, "Cannot claim staking incentives with the same parameters twice";
```
Output:
```bash
claimStakingIncentiveRule               |Violated  
```
Our scenario highlights a critical concern regarding the protocol's ability to prevent front-running attacks. Specifically, it focuses on ensuring that the claimStakingIncentives function cannot be abused by allowing repeated claims with identical parameters. The presence of this test and its failure suggests that the protocol may have a vulnerability that could be exploited by attackers to claim staking incentives more than once with the same parameters, potentially disrupting the fair distribution of rewards and undermining the protocol's security model.
## Tools Used
Formal verification
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Encrypt transaction details and only reveal them after the transaction is confirmed. This prevents observers from gaining an advantage by seeing the transaction details beforehand

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/registries/contracts/staking/StakingBase.sol#L864-L865


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Because the `StakingBase` never `approves` itself to spend `WETH`, the `token` transfer will always revert making it impossible to `unstake`

## Proof of Concept
In the `StakingBase.sol` contract whenever a user calls unstake to be able tp unstake their staked `tokens`, in this case `WETH`, it would fail as the `transfer` is done using the `safetransferFrom` method. As can be seen in the docs any `ERC20` token is accepted and the the deployment will also take place on Arbitrum.
`WETH` is a very popular token and will certainly be used for `staking`. The issue is that when `unstake` is called, the whole call will fail. 
```solidity
    IService(serviceRegistry).safeTransferFrom(address(this), msg.sender, serviceId);
```
The `safetransferFrom` method, will work fine on most `chains` which uses the standard `WETH9` contract that handles the case when `src == msg.sender`
```solidity
WETH9.sol
          If (src != msg.sender && allowance[src][msg.sender] !=uint(-1)) {
          require(allowance[src][msg.sender] >= wad);
allowance[src][msg.sender] -= wad;
}
```
The problem is that the `WETH` implementation on `Arbitrum` uses a [different contract](https://arbiscan.io/address/0x8b194beae1d3e0788A1a35173978001ACDFba668#code) and does not have `src == msg.sender` handling.
 
## Tools Used
Manual review 

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
--    IService(serviceRegistry).safeTransferFrom(address(this), msg.sender, serviceId);
++       IService(serviceRegistry).safeTransfer(address(this), msg.sender, serviceId);

ERC20

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/e2a8bc31d2769bfb578a06cc64919ad369a82c08/tokenomics/contracts/staking/WormholeDepositProcessorL1.sol#L82


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Refunds will be lost.

## Proof of Concept

In both L1 and L2 WormholeDepositProcessor contracts, if the refundAccount is not set, set it to the `msg.sender`.

```
        // If refundAccount is zero, default to msg.sender
        if (refundAccount == address(0)) {
            refundAccount = msg.sender;
        }
```

In this case, the `msg.sender` is eith the Dispenser or the DefaultTargetDispenserL2 contract. The function assumes that the L1 and L2 addresses is the same, so that the refund can go to the same address, just on different chain.

However, that might not be the case as the same contract may have a different address on a different chain. 0x123 on L1 may be 0x456 on L2, which means that the `msg.sender` will be of a different address. 

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Best is to not assume that contracts on a different chain have the same address, and make sure `refundAccount` is always set by the caller. It will be ideal if the `refundAccount` is reverted if it is address(0), instead of being the msg.sender.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
User funds will be locked
## Proof of Concept
In StakingBase, when a user calls the stake function to stake, if the reward in the contract is insufficient (availableRewards == 0), the user's stake call will be rolled back. Set the parameter MinStakingRewards

    revert NoRewardsAvailable();
  }

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/main/governance/contracts/VoteWeighting.sol#L657-L661


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
pointsSum will be incorrect.

## Detail
In the function `revokeRemovedNomineeVotingPower`, protocol will update the changesWeight and changesSum. However, this operation should be synchronized with the update of pointsSum. If the changesSum is reduced, the slope of pointsSum also should be reduced, or else the slope of pointsSum will be larger than expected after oldSlope.end.
On the other hand, the function `revokeRemovedNomineeVotingPower` doesn't update the slope of pointsSum in any case, but changesSum may be changed. Then, two situations will occur. The first situation is that changesSum is updated (decreased), so the slope of pointsSum will be reduced by a smaller value. The other situation is that changesSum is not updated, then the slope of pointsSum will be reduced by a larger value. The final result is that after `oldSlope.end`, pointsSum will have two possible values, which is obviously incorrect.

## Tools Used
VScode

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
When updating changesSum, the slope of pointsSum needs to be updated at the same time.

Math
